name: frontend-architect
description: Develop frontend requirements through connected architecture design, implementation and verification; review code against product contracts and the same engineering standard. Autonomously discover context and complete the requested delivery for web, app and mini-programs, including shared foundations and design-only work. Excludes backend-only work and visual assets without frontend code.

# Frontend Architect

Produce frontend changes that are easy to understand, safe to change, and
proportionate to the product need. Apply the same engineering standard when
implementing and reviewing; functional success alone does not prove code quality.

## Own the task from a short request

The user supplies the outcome and target, not a checklist of engineering duties.
Requirement development and architecture design form one feedback loop: product
rules and acceptance shape responsibilities, code contracts and data flow;
implementation and verification expose constraints that refine the design and
step sequence. A development request includes the applicable architecture work.
Infer the requested delivery boundary from context: complete development, a
design-only deliverable or review only. Discover relevant requirements, accepted decisions, code,
consumers and checks yourself; choose the needed guidance without waiting for the
user to name modularity, function design, state ownership, diagrams or review axes.
Ask only when a consequential choice remains unresolved after investigation;
continue independent work. Do not stop at a plan when implementation is requested.

Use the full applicable shared standard throughout development, design and review.
Task size changes scope, design detail and verification effort, not whether clarity,
correctness and maintainability matter. "Highest standard" does not justify invented
defects, speculative frameworks or claims beyond evidence. Respect an explicitly
limited scope and existing authorization; design-only and review-only requests do
not authorize implementation. Routine workflow selection needs no approval.

## Shared engineering standard

Apply these defaults to code, configuration, scripts and operations in scope:

- Understand existing contracts and maintenance workflows. Reuse project
  capabilities, standard tools and suitable maintained solutions; custom code
  fills a real gap. A native API is not simpler if it discards established policy.
- At real callers, an operation's name, inputs, result and effects should express
  one coherent responsibility. Keep APIs narrow and accurately typed, execution
  order visible, and helpers responsible for rules or complexity rather than
  renamed forwarding steps. Resolve mixed responsibilities before renaming.
- Give state, rules, effects, cleanup and errors explicit owners. Derive secondary
  values; keep genuinely atomic transitions together. Split at meaningful semantic,
  lifecycle or dependency boundaries. A page composes capabilities without moving
  every draft, request and subscription into one giant hook. Private helpers can
  stay with their owner; file length and layer count do not establish modularity.
- Anticipate common domain changes and caller needs before implementation, even
  without a roadmap or current duplication. Modest seams and convenient APIs
  should earn their cost through today's clarity or usability; generalized
  mechanisms need stronger evidence. Before delivery, trace a realistic follow-up
  change and improve a leaky boundary. This needs no separate report or approval.
- Defend actual trust boundaries and credible failures. Reuse existing guarantees;
  internal code can rely on validated contracts. Preserve authorization, external
  input constraints and secret protection; avoid repeated validation and swallowed
  errors. Client permission checks do not authorize privileged server operations.
- Preserve the intended observable contract, including errors and relevant
  accessibility, locale and lifecycle behavior. Distinguish that contract from an
  accidental defect; disclose observable changes and resolve material ambiguity.
  Complete affected consumers, types, checks and necessary documentation.
- Act autonomously within existing authorization. Investigate facts and continue
  independent reversible work; ask only about consequential choices the evidence
  cannot settle. Surface extra protection that materially changes the product or
  maintenance cost. Keep unrelated cleanup out of scope.

## Work from behavior to evidence

Establish the actor, trigger, outcome and meaningful branches; inspect the relevant
code, consumers and authoritative contracts. Model identities, minimal state,
transitions and effect owners, then connect a complete flow to a check that could
expose its failure. Shared rules must agree across the paths that implement them.
Revisit decisions when evidence changes; scale depth to uncertainty and impact.
For work that needs design, turn these checkpoints into the technical document
required below before changing implementation. Documentation adds no approval gate.

Follow the selected framework, router and repository conventions. Read relevant
existing domain definitions and decisions; visual similarity does not establish
semantics. Inspect a named upstream's contracts and maintenance flow. Verify
consequential unsettled version/API assumptions, while settled local edits need
no fresh survey. Use specialized skills for framework, platform or tool mechanics.
Communicate in the user's language and follow the project's language for code
comments and documentation.

| Requested work | Execution and completion |
| --- | --- |
| Clear local edit | Implement directly within established behavior and boundaries; check the affected outcome |
| Feature | Decompose requirements and design their supporting architecture together; save the initial technical design, implement and verify ordered increments, and reconcile contracts and diagrams with the evidence |
| Design-only delivery | Carry the same requirement-to-architecture work through an implementation-ready document with functional steps, code contracts and both diagrams; save and link it, distinguish proposed checks from executed evidence, and respect the requested stopping point |
| Defect | Reproduce the symptom, distinguish hypotheses, fix its responsible boundary and repeat the decisive check |
| Refactor or simplification | Preserve intended contracts; remove mechanisms serving abandoned requirements while retaining real consumers; verify surviving behavior |
| Shared foundation | Establish consumers and a narrow public contract; complete applicable types, diagnostics, artifacts, compatibility and consumer checks |
| Migration | Use an incremental seam, compatibility and recovery; retire the old path after evidence |
| Review only | Infer scope, discover requirement sources and assess both requirement compliance and the shared engineering standard; inspect real code and omissions, report evidenced findings and a bounded quality conclusion; do not edit implementation |

For a defect, distinguish symptom, hypothesis and demonstrated mechanism. Recovery
clearing a symptom does not establish the main-path cause. Retain justified
recovery, withdraw rejected experiments, and leave missing incident evidence
unresolved. When tests disagree with the application, inspect the harness and
real event/layout conditions before changing production code.

### Design before and during implementation

For new or changed business workflows, refactors that redistribute responsibilities,
shared foundations and migrations, create or update a technical document before
editing implementation, even when the user asks only for the feature. Read
[technical design](references/architecture-and-code.md#turn-requirements-into-an-executable-technical-design).
Decompose the requirement into an explicitly counted, dependency-ordered sequence;
map each step's functions or classes to its functionality, contracts and acceptance.
Include both a technical architecture diagram and a data-flow diagram. Keep this
design aligned with implementation and verification through delivery.

Use the shared engineering standard and relevant routed guidance to make these
decisions throughout development. Connect reuse, responsibility and dependency
boundaries, paradigm choice, state/resource ownership and realistic evolution to
the required behavior; include applicable runtime, trust, interface and performance
obligations. Preserve consequential choices, concrete reasons and checks in the
design. Assess engineering quality in both the proposal and actual implementation;
document completeness and passing behavior tests alone do not establish it.
Select the applicable depth yourself; topic names and prescribed patterns are not
a quota for every design.
Infer applicable methods from the requested behavior, even when the user names no
technique. Use the [behavior-to-design lenses](references/architecture-and-code.md#match-design-lenses-to-behavior)
before settling steps and contracts, then read the matching sections. For example,
spatial continuity during reordering calls for transition-mechanism evaluation,
including FLIP when geometry mapping is needed. Carry the selected method's
invariants, ownership and checks into the design and implementation.

A settled local edit that only follows established behavior and boundaries needs
no design document: for example a label, spacing token or existing filter binding.
Do not use file count or the absence of ambiguity to exempt a new business flow.
Investigation and read-only review need no implementation document unless requested;
an unexplained defect needs causal evidence before a proposed redesign.
Use the project's existing documentation location and relevant owned record; if
none exists, create a discoverable document. Scale detail to the actual requirement,
without waiting for document approval. Preserve useful decision reasons and history.

## Read only the needed sections

Start with this file alone for a clear local change. For an unresolved decision,
choose the matching section below; do not read an entire reference merely because
one section applies. Locate its heading and read through the next heading at the
same level, including relevant subsections. Reference contents help when the
match is uncertain. Read a whole topic when its interacting parts are needed.

Use headings to discover a relevant section; discovery is not a reason to load
its whole topic. Expand for a decision the task or inspected evidence actually
requires, then stop when enough is known to act. Reuse loaded guidance; topic
count is not a quota and routine routing needs no narrated reading checklist.
Ordinary validation does not require the verification reference, nor an ordinary
component update the rendering guide.

| Unresolved decision | Start here; follow further sections only as needed |
| --- | --- |
| Domain meaning or lasting decision | [Domain knowledge](references/architecture-and-code.md#preserve-domain-knowledge-and-decisions) |
| Function clarity, call contracts, utilities or local refactor | [Readable operations](references/architecture-and-code.md#construct-a-readable-operation); [utility contracts](references/architecture-and-code.md#design-utilities-around-explicit-contracts) for a general utility |
| State, data, component/API ownership or abstraction | [Architecture contents](references/architecture-and-code.md#contents), then the relevant section |
| Races, request policy, reconciliation or cleanup | [Async and lifecycles](references/async-and-lifecycles.md) |
| Application/feature organization or dependency direction | [Module contents](references/module-boundaries.md#contents), then the relevant scale |
| Functions, objects, closures, reducers or state machines | [Paradigm decision matrix](references/programming-paradigms.md#decision-matrix), then the relevant representation |
| Execution placement, routing, hydration, caches, bundles or rollout | [Runtime and delivery](references/runtime-and-delivery.md), select the relevant heading |
| Measured update-to-display, frames, lists, images or memory | [Rendering contents](references/rendering-and-performance.md#contents): common model and the relevant platform extension; multiple extensions only for an actual cross-platform difference |
| Libraries, SDKs, shared packages, build tools or versioned contracts | [Infrastructure contract](references/frontend-infrastructure.md#design-the-contract-before-the-internals), then applicable artifact, consumer and evolution obligations |
| Untrusted data, DOM sinks, permissions, secrets or third parties | [Security and trust](references/security-and-trust.md), select the actual boundary |
| Layout, interaction, accessibility or component systems | [Interface contents](references/interface-and-motion.md#contents), then the relevant behavior |
| Reordering, shared elements or interrupted spatial transitions | [Transition mechanism](references/interface-and-motion.md#choose-the-lightest-transition-mechanism); [FLIP](references/interface-and-motion.md#apply-flip-deliberately) when geometry mapping is needed |
| Requested review | [Scope and coverage](references/verification-and-review.md#establish-review-scope-and-coverage), [code quality](references/verification-and-review.md#review-architecture-and-implementation) and [findings](references/verification-and-review.md#report-findings-and-evidence); add interface/security/performance checks when applicable |
| Uncertain check, root cause, performance claim or durable evidence | [Verification contents](references/verification-and-review.md#contents), then the relevant section |

Resolve reference overlap through the least-complex coherent choice within task
and repository contracts. Named methods are conditional lenses, not overriding
authorities; applicable correctness and safety obligations still hold.

## Verify and report

Before delivering a design, inspect its proposed contracts, ownership and flows
against the same engineering standard; resolve evidenced design gaps and keep
unsettled facts explicit.
Before delivering implementation, inspect the actual changed code and affected
callers against the same engineering standard used in a requested review; remedy
in-scope defects and maintenance problems. Passing behavior checks is not this
code-quality check, and the check needs no separate review ceremony.

Choose checks that can expose the changed outcome at its real consumer boundary.
Check the consumer's settled outcome, not just that a handler ran: pending work,
accepted data, visible feedback, recovery and the final state after interruption
or teardown. Browser/device claims need that runtime; class names, synthetic
events or test counts do not prove layout, focus or performance. Measure material
optimizations before and after on representative conditions. Preserve user
preferences and relevant loading, empty, error, permission, stale, cancellation
and race behavior.

Open with the state decisive checks support: for example, "Implemented; browser
acceptance remains blocked." A request for a publishable or compatible foundation
sets a goal; claim that state only after its decisive checks pass. Packaging
success cannot establish unexercised behavior. A later caveat cannot qualify a
stronger headline. Keep the opening, summary and host-feedback rounds consistent; report
the achieved outcome, important choice, actual verification and gaps.
For reviews, put actionable findings by severity first and distinguish defects
from evidenced maintenance concerns. Keep lasting acceptance evidence in existing
project records and artifact storage; use [evidence maintenance](references/verification-and-review.md#keep-evidence-reproducible)
for lasting claims; reuse existing records rather than a new archive per edit.

When delivery is in scope, use the project's package manager, generation sources
and release/recovery paths. Check the core flow after an authorized deployment;
local validation or a release plan does not authorize publishing.

## Skill maintenance

Checking, updating or rolling back this installation uses the independently
installed `frontend-architect-update` companion when available; its source is
`skills/frontend-architect-update/SKILL.md`. Ordinary frontend work does not
trigger an update check. Skill development follows `CONTRIBUTING.md` in its source
repository.

# Product and order filters

This browser application uses native ES modules. `ui.mjs` contains the project's
labelled controls and buttons, and `query.mjs` provides the existing asynchronous
data access. Use the same public controls, data and URLs.

Products have keyword, category and publication status. Users edit a draft and
press Apply. Reset restores published/all categories/empty keyword. Orders have
keyword, date range and order status; a valid edit takes effect immediately.
Reset restores all statuses and the 30 calendar days ending on the project date
from `data.mjs`. Product and order status values describe different concepts.

The URL is the applied filter source. Keep unrelated parameters. Refresh and
browser history restore the appropriate applied fields. Product draft changes
must not start a query. Incomplete or reversed order dates remain editable and
show an associated error without changing the applied URL or results. Query
failures use a visible alert, and earlier responses cannot replace the current
result. Result counts describe the actual returned rows.

Keep the existing control labels, page links and Results list. Narrow containers,
long translated labels, keyboard operation and 200% text sizing must remain
usable without horizontal page overflow. Existing design-system functions in
ui.mjs may be extended while preserving their public behavior. There is no
animation or performance-optimization requirement. Run npm run check.

# Async Operations and Lifecycles

Use when request ordering, mutations, optimistic state, retries, subscriptions,
or owned resources are a real source of complexity. Use the project's existing
data layer or framework lifecycle when it already provides the required policy;
this reference is not a request to write a generic request engine.

## Choose policy from the operation

First establish what concurrent operations mean to the user and the server.

| Meaning | Suitable starting policy | What it does not guarantee |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Only the newest search or preview matters | Publish only the current request's result; optionally abort superseded work | Aborting does not prove the server stopped, and some clients ignore cancellation |
| Every local edit must be saved in order | Serialize writes or use server versions/conflict handling | A local queue does not order other tabs or devices |
| Repeated activation while pending should do nothing | Disable/guard the local command; server idempotency for duplicate effects | A disabled button alone does not prevent retries or multiple clients |
| Identical reads can share work | Existing cache/deduplication keyed by complete identity | Deduplication is not freshness, authorization or invalidation |
| Independent reads improve latency | Bounded parallel work and an explicit partial-failure policy | Promise aggregation does not make results atomic |
| A write timed out with unknown outcome | Reconcile with the authoritative source or retry with a supported stable idempotency key | Timeout is not proof of failure and unsafe writes must not be blindly repeated |

Do not apply latest-wins cancellation to an ordered save queue, or serialize all
searches when only the latest result matters. Debouncing reduces frequency; it
does not establish any of these correctness guarantees.

## Separate execution from publication

For a latest-result operation, the owner needs a stable input snapshot, a request
identity and a condition for publishing completion. Check that condition for
success, failure, and cleanup that changes visible state. An old `finally`
clearing `loading` can be wrong even if old success results are ignored.

Reason through a concrete timeline before implementing:

```text
submit A -> submit B -> B succeeds -> A fails
expected: B remains visible, A's error and cleanup do not replace B's state
```

Also cover A completing while B is still pending. Cancellation may save work;
identity/version checking determines whether completion is still relevant.
Use the data layer's query key and lifecycle if it already expresses this.
Do not add a parallel request counter, local loading flag and cache behind it.

An operation's identity can include resource, user/tenant, query and generation.
A response for the old account or route must not become current merely because
its promise resolves last. Define what dispose, navigation, replacement and
resubmission do to pending completion. A retry normally uses the failed submitted
input; editing a draft does not silently change the meaning of retry.

Keep the submitted input distinct from the editable draft. Completion may clear
the draft only if its owner and edit version still match the submitted operation;
equal text does not prove there were no intervening edits (A -> B -> A). Reuse
the form's existing revision or dirty lifecycle; add a local edit generation only
when needed, including programmatic edits such as clear. Do not lock the whole
editor to avoid an interaction the product must support.

## Keep errors actionable and owned

Catch at the layer that can recover, translate an external error into its public
contract, or present it. Do not catch in every helper, duplicate notifications,
or convert failure into an empty successful value. Expected validation or domain
rejection can be a typed result; unexpected transport/runtime failure can remain
an exception according to the project's convention. Do not introduce Result
wrappers throughout the project for one operation.

Keep enough context to identify the failed operation and recovery action without
leaking sensitive payloads. Differentiate cancellation caused by supersession
from a current user-visible failure. If recovery is impossible locally, retain
an honest error or unknown-result state rather than promising that retry is safe.

## Reconcile optimistic state with acknowledgements

Keep these meanings distinct when optimistic behavior exists:

- the last server-confirmed value/version;
- pending user intent and its operation identity;
- the projection currently shown to the user.

If save A is confirmed while save B is pending and B then fails, rollback must
reflect the newest valid acknowledgement, not an old closure snapshot. Define
whether server responses can be ordered by version; client request order alone
does not establish server commit order. When the contract cannot support safe
optimism, use pending feedback and authoritative refresh instead.

Rollback is a new decision against current state, not unconditional restoration
of everything captured before `await`. It must not undo another successful edit,
a later navigation, or changes to unrelated fields. Put related state changes
in one owned transition rather than updating competing stores independently.

## Own acquisition, replacement and release

A resource owner has one lifecycle from acquisition to release. Establish:

- who acquires, publishes and disposes it;
- what happens if acquisition fails partway through;
- how replacement invalidates the previous instance and pending callbacks;
- which cleanup operations are safe to repeat;
- whether a consumer is borrowing a shared resource or owns it exclusively.

A disposer returned by a subscription should remove that registration only.
Cleanup from an old component must not destroy a replacement owned by another
mount. Do not close a shared connection whenever one subscriber disappears.
Use framework cleanup where possible; choose a class/closure only if it makes
resource identity and lifecycle clearer than the existing owner.

## Verify the policy, not the machinery

Use controllable promises, clocks or transport boundaries to create meaningful
orders without arbitrary sleeps. Assert visible state and public side effects:
newer results survive old success/error/cleanup; ordered commands reach the
transport in the required order; an unknown write outcome is reconciled; disposal
prevents stale publication and releases only owned resources.

Use a real browser/device when the claim concerns navigation, native resources,
DOM interaction or layout. Unit-level race checks establish operation semantics,
not successful rendering or actual device cleanup. Keep production APIs narrow;
do not expose private counters or controllers merely to simplify a test.

## Turn requirements into an executable technical design

Use this section for the design-bearing work identified in SKILL.md. The document
connects requirement development with architecture and implementation. Derive
boundaries and code contracts from the functional steps and acceptance; use those
contracts to expose missing cases or dependencies in the decomposition. Revisit
both when implementation or verification reveals a constraint. Each refinement
must still serve the product outcome and its real consumers.

Establish the initial design after inspecting the relevant system and
before changing source, tests, configuration or generation templates. Inspection,
reproduction and baseline checks can precede it. Do not substitute a chat outline
or an after-the-fact description of finished code. Reuse a relevant owned document;
otherwise add one under the project's documentation convention and link it from
an existing discovery point when available. Missing documentation is a reason to
write the design, not to skip it or wait for an initialization session.

Apply the shared engineering standard while forming this design. Use the relevant
decision guidance to compare plausible choices against actual consumers, existing
capabilities, invariants and likely changes. For consequential choices, connect
the requirement or constraint, chosen boundary/representation, concrete reason
and a check or change scenario that can expose a poor choice. Put that reasoning
beside the affected contract or step in the same document; naming principles
does not demonstrate their application. A prescribed architecture, paradigm or
extra layer needs a reason in this system.

### Match design lenses to behavior

Discover applicable ideas from the behavior and constraints, without requiring the
user to name a method. This is a navigation map into existing decision guidance;
read the relevant sections and use their tradeoffs and stopping conditions.

| Requirement signal | Design lens and consequential decision | Guidance |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Features change independently or technical folders scatter one change | Colocation, information hiding and Feature-Sliced Design: choose owned feature boundaries, public APIs and dependency direction that fit this ecosystem | [Module grouping](module-boundaries.md#compare-the-two-grouping-strategies); [hide complexity](module-boundaries.md#hide-complexity-not-just-code) |
| Screens share controls or visual patterns but differ in product rules | Atomic Design and composition: identify stable parts and wholes, shared policy and product ownership | [Component-system boundaries](interface-and-motion.md#choose-component-system-boundaries) |
| Business rules mix with effects, identity or legal state transitions | Functional core/imperative shell, objects and reducers/state machines: choose representation per responsibility and lifecycle | [Paradigm choices](programming-paradigms.md#decision-matrix); [functional boundary](programming-paradigms.md#use-a-functional-core-and-imperative-shell-by-default) |
| UI facts duplicate source data or effects copy derived values | Minimal state and synchronization boundaries: derive facts, keep genuine edit state, give effects an external owner | [State model](#model-data-and-state); [forms](#model-forms-and-navigation-state) |
| Similar code or expected change suggests a shared abstraction | AHA and the wrong-abstraction lens: compare stable common semantics, caller convenience and change locality | [Abstraction timing](#abstract-at-the-right-time) |
| Content, translations, zoom or available space vary | Intrinsic layout, inclusive interaction and progressive enhancement: use content constraints, native semantics and a supported baseline | [Layout constraints](interface-and-motion.md#design-layout-from-content-and-constraints); [resilient baseline](interface-and-motion.md#build-the-semantic-and-resilient-layer-first); [locale](interface-and-motion.md#control-styles-and-internationalized-content) |
| Reordering, expansion or shared elements must preserve spatial continuity | Compare the lightest transition mechanism; use FLIP when measured geometry must map old to new layout | [Mechanism choice](interface-and-motion.md#choose-the-lightest-transition-mechanism); [First/Last/Invert/Play](interface-and-motion.md#apply-flip-deliberately) |
| Input response, motion, loading, frames or memory are problematic | RAIL and update-to-display cost: localize work, invalidation, transfer, layout/paint or resource cost on the actual runtime | [Perceived response](interface-and-motion.md#protect-accessibility-and-performance); [rendering model](rendering-and-performance.md#model-the-path-from-update-to-display) |
| Async results race, optimistic edits fail or resources outlive a view | Execution versus publication, ordering and acknowledgement: choose current-result or ordered-command policy, reconcile authority and own acquisition/release | [Async policy](async-and-lifecycles.md#choose-policy-from-the-operation); [reconciliation](async-and-lifecycles.md#reconcile-optimistic-state-with-acknowledgements); [resource ownership](async-and-lifecycles.md#own-acquisition-replacement-and-release) |
| Data crosses environments or caches represent remote facts | Runtime placement and cache ownership: define serialization, scope, authority, freshness and invalidation | [Environment boundaries](runtime-and-delivery.md#map-environments-before-components); [cache owner](runtime-and-delivery.md#give-every-cache-an-owner) |
| Untrusted content or privileged actions cross a boundary | Source-to-sink reasoning and server authorization: reuse established guarantees and protect the actual trust boundary | [Data path](security-and-trust.md#trace-data-from-source-to-sink); [authorization](security-and-trust.md#separate-presentation-from-authorization) |
| A capability becomes a shared package, SDK or tool | Contract-first design and consumer evolution: define public types/artifacts, compatibility and verification at real consumers | [Infrastructure contract](frontend-infrastructure.md#design-the-contract-before-the-internals); [public artifact](frontend-infrastructure.md#verify-the-public-artifact) |

Selecting a lens means applying its decision rules, not adding its name or folder
template to the document. Preserve the original method's conditional scope: FLIP
is appropriate only when its visual relationship and measurement needs exist;
Atomic Design and Feature-Sliced Design do not mandate directory trees; RAIL
does not prove performance or impose a universal frame budget. Other tasks may
need other sections from the existing topic navigation.

For a selected motion method, make the visual contract part of the functional
steps: underlying business/DOM state, geometry or snapshot data, interruption,
cleanup, reduced motion and real-runtime verification must have owners. Likewise,
carry each other selected lens's material constraints into contracts and checks.
Do not force every lens into a local edit or narrate a rejected-method checklist.

## Model data and state

Store the minimal, complete set of information the interface must remember.
Derive everything else where it is consumed.

Before adding state, ask:

1. Does it change over time?
2. Is it already supplied by props, a store, the URL, a form, cache, or server?
3. Can it be calculated from existing values?
4. Is another state variable representing the same fact?
5. What event owns the transition?
6. Can the proposed representation express contradictory states?

Prefer a representation such as:

```ts
type LoadState<T> =
  | { status: 'idle' }
  | { status: 'loading' }
  | { status: 'success'; data: T }
  | { status: 'error'; error: Error }
```

over unrelated booleans such as `isLoading`, `isSuccess`, and `isError` when
those booleans can contradict one another. Do not introduce a state machine for
a two-state local toggle; use it when transitions, concurrency, or invalid
combinations are actually difficult.

Keep state close to the smallest common owner of the consumers. Promote it only
when multiple consumers need shared coordination, persistence, or routing.

## Model forms and navigation state

Treat a non-trivial form as a workflow, not a bag of controlled inputs. Separate:

- editable draft values from server-authoritative values;
- derived display values from persisted fields;
- touched, dirty, validating, submitting, succeeded, and failed states when the
  product distinguishes them;
- client feedback from authoritative server validation and field or form errors;
- synchronous constraints from asynchronous checks that can race or become stale.

Keep submission idempotency, duplicate activation, cancellation, draft recovery,
and unsaved-navigation behavior explicit when failure would lose work or create
duplicate effects. Map server errors to fields only when the server contract
provides stable field identity; otherwise preserve a form-level recovery path.
Do not introduce a form library merely because a form exists, but use the
project's established form model when it already owns these lifecycles.

State belongs in the URL when users must be able to bookmark, share, reload, or
navigate back and forward through it. Define one parser and serializer with
defaults, validation, canonical ordering, and unknown-value behavior. Decide
which changes create history entries and which replace the current entry. Keep
ephemeral input, secrets, and large drafts out of URLs. Verify initial server and
client interpretation, `popstate` or router navigation, focus, scroll restoration,
and interactions between URL state and cached data when those behaviors apply.

## Place behavior by ownership

- Pure transformation belongs near the domain data or use site.
- User-event logic belongs in the event path that explains why it ran.
- Synchronization with a browser API, network subscription, timer, external
  widget, or other external system belongs at an explicit effect boundary.
- Data access belongs behind a boundary that makes loading, cancellation,
  caching, and errors observable.
- Presentation components should not silently own cross-page policy.

An effect is not a general-purpose place to react to any state change. If a
value can be calculated during rendering, derive it. If logic is caused by a
specific user action, keep it in that event path. Always define subscription
cleanup and consider stale responses or remounting.

## Build the semantic and resilient layer first

Start with the simplest layer that communicates the content and supports the
primary task:

1. Semantic HTML and native browser behavior.
2. CSS for layout, presentation, and supported state expression.
3. JavaScript for behavior the platform layer cannot provide alone.
4. Framework and advanced enhancement where product complexity justifies them.

Progressive enhancement does not require every experience to work identically
without JavaScript. It requires a deliberate baseline and avoids turning an
optional enhancement failure into total loss of content or control when a
resilient fallback is practical.

Prefer native controls when their semantics and behavior fit. A custom control
inherits responsibility for keyboard operation, focus, disabled behavior,
labels, form participation, and assistive-technology semantics.

## Design layout from content and constraints

Prefer intrinsic and container-aware layout over device-specific pixel patches.

- Let content, available space, and min/max constraints participate in sizing.
- Use Grid, Flexbox, logical properties, `minmax()`, `clamp()`, and container
  queries when supported and appropriate.
- Add breakpoints where the content or interaction breaks, not for a catalog of
  device widths.
- Preserve document order and reading order; do not use visual reordering to
  create an inaccessible focus sequence.
- Test narrow, wide, zoomed, translated, and long-content states.
- Avoid fixed heights for text-bearing regions unless overflow behavior is part
  of the design.

CSS is a constraint system, not a list of screenshots. Prefer rules that explain
the intended relationship between elements.

## Choose component-system boundaries

Use design-system primitives for stable visual and behavioral policy: tokens,
typography, spacing, controls, focus treatment, and common interaction patterns.
Keep product-specific meaning in product components.

Atomic Design is a useful lens for seeing both the whole interface and reusable
parts. It is not a mandatory folder hierarchy. Promote a component into a shared
system only when it has stable cross-context semantics, documented variants,
accessibility behavior, and an owner for future change.

Avoid a universal component whose API is a long list of flags. Prefer:

- clear variants for a coherent concept;
- slots or composition for structural differences;
- separate components when behavior and reasons for change diverge;
- tokens for controlled visual choices rather than arbitrary values everywhere.

## Control styles and internationalized content

Give CSS the smallest practical ownership boundary. Prefer project-native
scoping, semantic tokens, and documented public styling hooks. Keep global
resets, utility layers, component styles, product overrides, and third-party CSS
in an intentional cascade order; use cascade layers only when the supported
environment and existing system can adopt them coherently. Avoid specificity
escalation, arbitrary global selectors, and private DOM selectors as consumer
APIs. Verify themes, forced colors, zoom, long content, and token changes at the
real consuming boundary.

Do not concatenate translatable sentences or assume word order, string length,
or a left-to-right layout. Use message keys with locale-aware plural selection
and platform or established-project formatters for dates, times, numbers, and
currencies. Set document or subtree language, use logical CSS properties, and
test bidirectional content when RTL or mixed-direction text is supported.
When rendered output varies by locale or timezone, make them explicit inputs at
server/client boundaries so hydration does not depend on each environment's
defaults.

## Specify interaction as behavior

For each interactive element, define:

- trigger and expected outcome;
- mouse, touch, and keyboard operation;
- focus entry, movement, restoration, and escape behavior;
- disabled versus unavailable semantics;
- loading, success, error, undo, and retry feedback;
- repeated activation and interruption behavior;
- behavior under slow network or partial rendering;
- announcements needed for dynamic updates.

Use established accessible patterns for dialogs, menus, listboxes, tabs,
tooltips, comboboxes, and disclosures. ARIA does not repair incorrect interaction
behavior; prefer native semantics and verified patterns.

For interactions that close, unmount or transfer focus, observe the result after
native defaults and rendering have settled. Restoring focus in a callback can
still be undone later in the same pointer sequence. Fix the responsible event
or lifecycle boundary while preserving consumer cancellation; do not globally
cancel pointer defaults to make a single check pass.
